method: Jump height is either entered directly as a jump-and-reach score or derived from a measured flight time on the kinematic relation for a vertical projectile, using g = 9.80665 m/s2: a jump that leaves the ground at v rises to h = v^2/(2g) and returns after t = 2v/g, so a flight time t corresponds to h = g*t^2/8 and the takeoff velocity is sqrt(2gh). Height, flight time and takeoff velocity are therefore three views of one jump and cannot disagree, and the same numbers are used for the power estimates. Peak power comes from two published regressions on squat-jump height in centimetres and body mass in kilograms: Sayers et al. (1999), 60.7 x height + 45.3 x mass - 2055, and Harman et al. (1991), 61.9 x height + 36.0 x mass - 1822. The Sayers equation is the headline figure because it was cross-validated on a larger and more varied sample, and the Harman result is shown beside it so the two estimates and their spread are visible; no averaging or ranking is invented. Both regressions were fitted to jump-and-reach scores against force-plate measurements, so they estimate mechanical power at takeoff within a few hundred watts and do not measure force, rate of force development, jump strategy or asymmetry. Metric input is centimetres and kilograms, imperial input is inches and pounds with 2.54 cm per inch and 0.45359237 kg per pound, flight time is always in seconds, and the units are converted before any arithmetic. Jump height is accepted from 5 to 150 cm (2 to 59 in), flight time from 0.10 to 1.20 s, and body mass from 20 to 300 kg (44 to 661 lb); decimal commas are accepted and blank, non-numeric, exponent-notation and out-of-range values are refused with the failing field named. A height-and-mass pair at which either regression returns a non-positive power is refused rather than shown as a negative or zero figure. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: S. P. Sayers, D. V. Harackiewicz, E. A. Harman, P. N. Frykman and M. T. Rosenstein, Cross-validation of three jump power equations, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 31(4):572-577, 1999: squat-jump peak power = 60.7 x jump height (cm) + 45.3 x body mass (kg) - 2055.

E. A. Harman, M. T. Rosenstein, P. N. Frykman, R. M. Rosenstein and W. J. Kraemer, Estimation of human power output from vertical jump, Journal of Applied Sport Science Research 5(3):116-120, 1991: peak power = 61.9 x jump height (cm) + 36.0 x body mass (kg) - 1822.

Evaluation of power prediction equations: peak vertical jumping power in women, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research: the same Harman and Sayers coefficients with the Harman constant subtracted, which is the form the published regressions use.
Standard projectiles kinematics: flight time t = 2 sqrt(2h/g) and takeoff velocity sqrt(2gh) for a jump with equal rise and fall times, with g = 9.80665 m/s2.
